narrative.text: Acknowledges the contributors to the manual and gives its table of contents.
A list of abbreviations used in the manual, mostly names of health programmes, departments and vaccines.

Introduces the manual as a concise, practical primer on developing health management information systems (HMIS) for readers without time for in-depth study. It describes the intended users and explains that the closing examples show how indicators and data flows can be presented rather than prescribing a model.
Defines key terms such as information system and HMIS and lists the ten steps for developing an HMIS, from reviewing the existing system to enhancing it.

Sets out the steps for reviewing an existing HMIS, including inventorying forms, assessing data quality and identifying problems in other components. It advises building on existing strengths rather than discarding systems, and the extracted text runs into steps for defining indicators. The page layout has been flattened, so headings appear broken up.

Covers defining data needs, matching information functions to administrative levels from village to national. It lists common issues, such as poorly defined roles and staff difficulty identifying indicators, and steps for finding data sources for indicators. It advises keeping detailed data at the source and limiting reporting to higher levels.

Discusses determining HMIS data flow, listing issues such as limited capacity at lower levels to summarize data and problems storing or retrieving raw data. It recommends drawing a flow chart of information from peripheral to national level. The text also runs into steps for drafting, pretesting and revising new forms and their instruction manual.

Gives principles for designing simple, short data collection and reporting tools suited to staff capability, with a sample worksheet defining a fully immunized child. It also touches on planning a pretest and specifying software requirements for reports, quality checks and analysis.

Sets out steps for HMIS data processing, which should match the objectives of data collection and analysis, including developing or adapting software and pretesting it for bugs and usability. The text then moves into designing training based on a needs assessment. It names the elements to define for training: target group, content, strategies and duration.

Describes developing HMIS training programmes suited to each target group, with a syllabus as output. It covers preparing and reproducing training materials such as a data dictionary and manuals for data providers and users, and planning evaluation in advance. A sample session plan for an introductory health statistics course is included.

Explains how to plan a pretest of the HMIS by deciding where, who, what and how, including criteria for selecting sites. The text then lists steps for monitoring and evaluation, from prioritizing activities to documenting results and making recommendations.

Covers monitoring and evaluating the HMIS, stressing that the aim is to find what works as well as what went wrong. It names issues such as institutionalizing evaluation and finding expertise, and gives a worksheet of variables to assess, including data quality, use, computing and training. The text then moves to planning HMIS expansion and resourcing, describing HMIS development as continuous improvement.

Lists steps for enhancing an HMIS, such as prioritizing options, scheduling and monitoring new components, and issues such as sustaining stakeholder interest and coordinating donors to avoid duplicate forms. It ends with a sample budget and two-year timetable showing costs and funding sources.

Introduces two examples, a list of indicators with data sources, collection methods and frequency, and a flow chart of the HMIS of a hypothetical country. It explains that both show how to present such information rather than prescribing content. The latter part of the extracted text is garbled symbols, apparently from the flow chart.
A reference list citing works on information systems management and WHO and Western Pacific regional guidance on health information systems and indicators.
The cover, title and cataloguing page of a WHO Western Pacific Regional Office practical guide on developing health management information systems, with ISBN, copyright and disclaimer text.
